‘Obsession’ is sure to terrify and intrigue

Curry Barker’s debut film demonstrates the horrors of unconditional love.
Vinny White, Arts and Culture Writer
July 13, 2026
Hadley Bierma / Daily Emerald

*Spoilers ahead

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:19
Instaread

Curry Barker’s terrifyingly engrossing horror film “Obsession” is nothing short of impressive. The director has experience with horror shorts, yes, but a debut film so tight, captivating and successful, coming from someone largely known for comedy sketches on YouTube, is a testament to how enough creativity can defy expectations. Having just finished its monumental theatrical run as one of the most profitable films of all time, it’s now available on digital, and is certainly worth watching.

“Obsession” follows Bear (Michael Johnston), a mild-mannered member of a friend group of music store employees, as he uses a mysterious “One Wish Willow” to garner the unrelenting love of his friend, Nikki (Inde Navarrette). He’s left to deal with the consequences of this action as Nikki gradually turns into something she is not, while his friends Ian (Cooper Tomlinson) and Sarah (Megan Lawless) are faced with the consequences.

The catalyst of the story, the “One Wish Willow,” is an overt plot device that needs little explanation. It’s a device that grants any wish with no strings attached. Bear, though seemingly harmless at the beginning of the movie, uses the wish for strictly selfish means and only continues to grow more selfish as time goes on. Johnston’s portrayal of Bear is wonderfully layered, accurately portraying the mannerisms of a manipulative loser who managed to worm his way into an otherwise-sound friend group. His character is easy to hate, yet he has a certain softness and occasional empathetic glances that makes the audience hope for a way out of his situation.

Starring alongside Johnston is Navarrette, who gives a tantalizing performance that brilliantly rides the line between horrifying and sympathy-inducing. Her character early in the film is immediately charming, which makes watching her voice and body language change as she succumbs to the wish all the more terrifying. The way her vocal patterns completely change, as do the accompanying crying, screaming and other miscellaneous noises, makes her feel like a completely different person than the one seen at the beginning of the film.


Lawless’ character is less prevalent than the rest, but her subplot about trying to get into college grounds the story and gives her more emotional weight. Tomlinson, a holdover from his and Barker’s YouTube comedy project, “that’s a bad idea,” provides a crucial comedic styling to the film. He hams it up a bit too much in the earlier portions of the movie, but as the chaos unfolds, he fits into the role believably.

The use of heavy-handed comedy is the secret ingredient that makes this film work. Some scenes feel ripped straight out of a “that’s a bad idea” sketch, with many of the funniest scenes simply portraying a few characters arguing over the semantics of the situation they’re in. While some may be afraid to laugh given the movie’s prevalence of tragic subjects, ignoring the dark-comedy threaded within this horror-drama would certainly be an oversight.

The camera work certainly aids the horror elements of this film, since its 3:2 aspect ratio creates a claustrophobic look that ensures the viewer is aware of everything on screen. Jump scares — at least cheap ones — are rare, since the camera work often makes it obvious what scares are coming next. Still, the pictures on screen are sure to cast many eyes to the floor. “Obsession” is generally enjoyable to look at, with solid camera work and cool colors that makes the gore all the more jarring. This is excluding a short, largely-comedic, effects-forward scene toward the end, which is oddly unconvincing for an otherwise visually sound film.

The film’s use of sound, particularly screaming, is what really sends shivers down the spine. This sound, as well as a complementary and wonderfully atmospheric score from Rock Burwell, makes even watching with closed eyes uncomfortable.

Even without the hype of a novice director making it big with his first feature, “Obsession” is a brilliant film. It knows when to go all the way and when to draw back. The characters all feel developed and exude an unspoken history. It’s not for the faint of heart, with the performance of Navarrette sure to linger in the mind of most long after they’ve left the theater — but there’s nothing wrong with being a little obsessed.
